summary: Presents a timeline of the history of the Internet, highlighting key events and technologies that shaped it, along with a growth summary. It is informational and was written in the 1990s, so it covers only that era.

plainLanguage.summary: It is a calendar that shows the big moments in how the Internet grew up, from the beginning to the 1990s.

questions: how many internet hosts were there in 1997
subtitle: A year-by-year timeline of Internet history from 1957 to 1997, with growth tables for hosts, the Web and Usenet.

tldr.problem: People who build and use the Internet often lack a compact record of how it came about and how fast it grew.
tldr.mechanism: The memo excerpts the author's Hobbes' Internet Timeline: dated entries from 1957 to 1997 grouped by decade, followed by growth tables for hosts, networks, domains, countries, Web sites and Usenet.
tldr.outcome: It is a snapshot of the history as known in November 1997, and not a specification. It also lists the sources and the contributors who supplied items.

today: RFC 2235 is an Informational memo (FYI 32) with no recorded replacement or update. It covers only events up to 1997, so it is a historical record and not a current account.

sections.title: What the Timeline Is
sections.content:
RFC 2235 (FYI 32) presents a history of the Internet in timeline fashion, highlighting key events and technologies, together with a growth summary of the Internet and some associated technologies. It is excerpted from the author's copyrighted work of the same name, and the memo says the most current version was kept online at the address it gives.

Many entries carry a code in the form (:amk:), which are the initials of the contributor who supplied the item. The memo's acknowledgements list who they are. The memo is informational and does not specify an Internet standard of any kind.
sections.plainLanguage: It is a scrapbook of Internet history, and the initials at the end of an entry show which friend helped add it.

sections.title: From ARPA to the Commercial Internet
sections.content:
The timeline opens in 1957, when the USSR launched Sputnik and the US formed ARPA within the Department of Defense in response. In 1962 Paul Baran wrote about packet-switching networks with no single outage point, and in 1969 the ARPANET was commissioned, with its first node at UCLA. The same year saw the first Request for Comment, "Host Software" by Steve Crocker.

The 1970s bring Network Control Protocol, email (invented by Ray Tomlinson in 1971), the Telnet and File Transfer specifications, Cerf and Kahn's 1974 paper on a Transmission Control Program, UUCP, and Usenet in 1979. In 1982 DCA and ARPA established TCP and IP as the protocol suite for ARPANET, and the cutover from NCP to TCP/IP happened on 1 January 1983. The Domain Name System was introduced in 1984, and NSFNET was created in 1986 with a 56Kbps backbone, later upgraded to T1 in 1988 and T3 in 1991.

The 1990s entries cover the end of ARPANET in 1990, the release of Gopher and the World-Wide Web in 1991, the chartering of the Internet Society in 1992, the 1993 arrival of Mosaic, and NSFNET reverting to a research network in 1995 as traffic moved to interconnected network providers.
sections.plainLanguage: It starts with a satellite scare that made the US fund new science, grows through the first computer links and email, and ends with the Web making the Internet popular.

sections.title: Other Networks, Incidents and Culture
sections.content:
The timeline is not only about ARPANET and the TCP/IP network. It also notes parallel networks such as BITNET, CSNET, EUnet, FidoNet and Minitel, and records which countries connected to NSFNET each year.

It includes incidents and social events too. The Internet worm of 2 November 1988 affected about 6,000 of the 60,000 hosts then on the Internet, and CERT was formed in response. Other entries include an unwanted email advertisement in 1994, SYN attacks that shut down the PANIX network in 1996, and a July 1997 corrupted DNS table at Network Solutions that made millions of systems unreachable. Fun items such as the Internet Toaster of 1990 also appear, and the author mixes in books like True Names and Neuromancer.
sections.plainLanguage: The calendar also lists funny things, scary bugs and other networks that grew up beside the Internet.

sections.title: The Growth Tables
sections.content:
After the timeline come tables. Internet growth lists dates with numbers of hosts, networks and domains. It starts with 4 hosts in 1969 and reaches 19,540,000 hosts, with 1,301,000 domains, in 07/97. A Worldwide Networks Growth table counts the countries reached by the Internet, BITNET, UUCP, FidoNet and OSI, for example 171 countries on the Internet by 07/97.

The WWW growth table runs from 130 sites in 06/93 to 1,364,714 in 09/97, and the USENET growth table runs from 3 sites in 1979 to 330,000 sites in 1995. The Usenet table marks MB and posts per day as approximate. The sources section names the zone reports, connectivity table and web growth summaries used to compile each table.
sections.plainLanguage: The charts count how many computers, countries and web sites joined, and the numbers shoot up very fast.
